questions.question: Describe the steps taken against Jewish people in Germany between April 1933 and September 1935, and explain why many Germans accepted them.
questions.expected_answer: April 1933: national boycott of Jewish shops; the civil service law dismissed Jewish civil servants; quotas on Jewish students; Jewish lawyers, doctors and journalists restricted; books burned in May 1933; anti-Jewish signs in public places. Acceptance came from constant propaganda, older antisemitic prejudice, the gradual and legal appearance of each step, fear of the Gestapo and camps, and self-interest of those who gained jobs or property.

questions.question: Explain the two Nuremberg Laws of September 1935 and what the definition of who was Jewish reveals about Nazi race theory.
questions.expected_answer: The Reich Citizenship Law made only people of German or related blood citizens, so Jews became subjects without the vote or public office. The Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour banned marriages and relationships between Jews and other Germans and forbade Jews to employ German women under 45. Jewishness was defined by the religion of grandparents (three or four Jewish grandparents meant Jewish), which shows there was no biological basis for the supposed race.

questions.question: Name four groups other than Jews who were persecuted by the Nazis and describe how each was treated.
questions.expected_answer: Roma and Sinti: classified as racially inferior, subjected to the marriage ban, interned and later murdered in genocide. People with disabilities: about 400 000 forcibly sterilised, and from 1939 murdered in the T4 programme. Gay men: convicted under a harsher 1935 law and sent to camps with pink triangles. Jehovah's Witnesses: imprisoned for refusing loyalty oaths and military service. Political opponents: sent to camps from 1933. Black Germans: forcibly sterilised in 1937.
